title: Is it possible to understand Persona (1966) by myself?

commenti.body: This is not an answerable question. We don't know you, your mental capacity, your film literacy, what you got out of it on first viewing, your experience with abstract film, absolutely nothing. It's not a video game where you get a new puzzle piece every time. I understand the desire to want to "figure it out on your own," but most people who are really into film and film studies aren't figuring it out all on their own. They're reading tons of texts, different interpretations from other people, interviews with the filmmakers, speaking with friends who have seen the movie, etc.

I get what you're saying, but I fear that by checking other people's opinions on the movie I won't form my own, and I'll just be regurgitating what I've read or seen online. 


Perhaps the question wasn't as properly framed as I'd like it to be (after all, english is not my first language) but what I'm trying to get at is... have you? Has the majority of the people that has seen this movie get what it is about? Or am I just dumb?

I understood it, but wanted to confirm and understand it more after watching it so I read up on the plot and things after watching. There’s nothing wrong with using resources to help further understand a movie
[removed]

I'd say watch it a few times and allow yourself time in between to think about it. At that point if you're still feeling in the dark, there is nothing wrong with reading some analysis of the film.

I saw it as part of a film course so I'll never know how much I would get out of it on my own, but I'll say that it's not the kind of film where there's a single "aha" revelation that will make it all cohere into a single interpretation.

Well that depends on your approach towards the films in general. Do you approach them as a detective riddle that needs to be solved or as an art piece that has to be felt rather than understood? Why do you need to have film *explained* to you?

What i wanted to say, in my opinion films are, in the end, subjective experience. Now let me be clear, that does not mean that it is entirely subjective if the room is superior film to 2001. There are tons of technical details that make 2001 one of the greatest movies ever and the room not so much. But then again, what matters the most (for you) is "how did the film make you feel"? And it is entirely possible that you felt stronger emotions with room than with 2001.

Back to Persona, it is probably one of the richest films in the history of the cinema. There are many (different) interpretations of every part of the movie, but that doesnt matter.  What matters is - do you like? How do you feel about it on subconciouss level? 

Now that doesnt mean that you shouldnt analyse and read about it. You should and thats how you learn more about the films and cinema itself. But what i would do and what i always do is sort of "heart first, brain later" approach. In my first/second viewing I immerse myself in the film and let it wash over me, without any prior knowledge. I form my opinion if i liked it. And only then, before second/third rewatch i read more about it, explore all objective and technical details, read about different interpretations and then i watch it again with all that knowledge on mind.

For Persona, as i said, it is one of the richest films ever, so in your place I would watch it once more with no explanations (that could spoil your viewing) and just enjoy it without overanalyzing. You will pick up a lot of stuff that way, and then read the analysis.

Hope that helps

Well, yeah, it's obviously possible that you can eventually get *an understanding* of the film. We all get our own interpretation of these things. Your understanding might be different to ours, or those that made the film, but you'll understand it. You'll potentially never understand why Ingmar Bergman made the film, or what he meant by its various points, but I don't think this is a fair aim. At least by yourself. Obviously if you watch an interview, or read a book/article, by a film critic then you'll get their understanding/interpretation. However, it's not guaranteed that this is correct. Ultimately the only way to fully understand it is to watch/read an interview or article by Bergman himself on what he intended. 

Sometimes, trying to understand a movie is a bit like recognising the tasting notes on a whisky or wine. You'll get the broad strokes but not the complex notes. However, with practice you'll get better at discerning the complex or hidden stuff. 

Finally, upon finding out what Bergman intended, if you can, you'll fully understand! Let me know when you figure it out! 

However, you might think it has a different message, or it might have a different effect on you that Bergman never intended/anticipated and that's okay too.

Yeah, I try to firstly *feel* the film, as you say, and then, later, analyse it. I definitely liked Persona as an art piece, and I usually enjoy surreal and complex filmmaking, even if I don't understand it in a first watching. 


But I also think that trying to interpret what I'm seeing or to search for a deeper meaning can sometimes elevate my opinion of a film, or make me feel closer to it in a way. I also think it can be an exercise to further understand other surreal movies in the future. 


But, my opinion of a film is always about what it says on an emotional level. The intellectual aspect is a way of... furthering the connection, if it's possible.

First off, you're not dumb! I think artists/filmmakers who explore kind of meta concepts are on the less accessible end of the art spectrum. Intent and message becomes a lot more layered.

>I fear that by checking other people's opinions on the movie I won't form my own, and I'll just be regurgitating what I've read or seen online. 

I think this is more of a personal issue than a film literacy thing, really. A lack of self-confidence, maybe. I always find that my opinions on movies are strengthened after discussing them with friends, but if I don't have anyone to discuss one with, reading other people's opinions can be similar. Sometimes after watching a movie, I'll have an impression and a feeling from it that I can't quite pin down. Looking at quality reviews or other people's takes can help me put it into words, and that can be helpful.

I also think it's worth pointing out that there's no rule that you have to have a fully formed opinion on a movie after one viewing. Some things need to be studied to be best understood. Bergman movies definitely fall into that category.

One thing you could do if you want to turn it into an exercise is watch a film, then ask yourself some basic questions. Maybe "what feelings do I have after watching this," "why do I feel that way," and "do I like that the film made me feel that way" and write down your responses. Then you could look at other people's opinions/reviews and ask yourself if you agree or disagree with them, or if they change your opinion of the film.

I may have explained it poorly, because I completely agree with you: there isn't an universal interpretation, or a *correct* interpretation, each one has their own and that's the beauty of art, it affects everyone differently. 


What makes me afraid, perhaps, is not finding my own interpretation, being illiterate in a way, not being able to find what it made **me** feel, or how I read it. 


I'm just rambling at this point, I'm sorry if I'm not making any sense.

Yeah, perhaps a lack of self confidence in my ability to... how do I say it... verbalise or express what I'm getting from each movie. Of course I have a reaction, and a... *subconscious* interpretation, but it's hard for me to understand it sometimes, maybe because I'm not that good at interpreting art.


Probably because I'm a maths major, sometimes it's hard for me to understand that, with this kind of things, there isn't a truth that needs to be found.

>"heart first, brain later"

I'm a big fan of this approach! I think it's kinda similar to what David Lynch has said (I think he said it, or else I read it written about his movies) about how his movies should be felt, not followed. 

Non-Lynch example: when I watched *I Saw the TV Glow*, I felt the most intense, visceral wave of grief after the ending. Exploring why I felt grief of all things made the experience of the film so much more powerful (I'm *so* impressed with Schoenbrun's ability to pull that reaction out of my cis ass and make me feel the agony of living an entire life without embracing oneself). The Beast/La Bête was another great one this year that offered a similar experience.

No need to apologise, it makes complete sense. We all start as illiterate, do we not? You just have to learn. Don't fear reading an article, and relying on other people's opinions, to begin. That'll teach you what you are looking for and how to translate it, if that makes sense.  After this it'll be easier to make your own interpretations. In a small way, you are kinda trying to read before you know how to, so don't be hard on yourself. 

By the way, I want to say that I'm not an expert, I still have to read stuff to fully understand these kinds of films. I likely always will.

I don’t think Persona is a movie that you need to understand or even have a clear interpretation of. Much like a lot of art cinema, its goal is to make you think and feel a certain way. You may arrive at an interpretation of your own eventually, but if you were moved by the style and narrative of the film, then the film did its job.

It's a psychological film evident by the [film's title.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persona_(psychology)) Meaning, you'd have to familiarize yourself with Freud and Jung, specifically the former's theories on psychoanalysis and psychosexual development: id, ego, super ego. How the two women's faces overlap is a clue concerning a deeper relationship, but that is all I will say since you don't want an explanation. Fortunately, a cursory wikipedia-entry-understanding, couple YouTube videos, and some ELI5 threads on psychology are more than sufficient to get what's going on. It's just half a day's research.

You should also watch Bergman's other film "Hour of the Wolf" as it is more straightforward and borrows a lot from Persona's psychological themes. You'll find the same multi-layered but very subtle break in reality that is in Persona. It's hard to explain without getting into detail, but it makes for a great companion piece, especially if you find Persona confusing.

All of our ideas are built off of outside ideas. Very rarely do we come up with things entirely on our own. Everything is informed by all that came before it. You didn't figure out math all by yourself, you were taught by people who knew more than you, and you studied the research done by millenia of mathematicians before you. Now that you've done the research and have the knowledge and tools, you have the ability to come up with your own ideas and proofs based on what you already know. It's the same with art. You can't expect to figure it out all by yourself without studying those that came before you. Start with people like Roger Ebert or Pauline Kael, or hell even just the reviews you find on Letterboxd. Get as many perspectives as you can, but be critical and attentive. Use your intuition to interpret other peoples' interpretations and see if they ring true to you. Take what you agree with, interrogate what you disagree with, and form your own opinion based on that. Write your thoughts and try to piece together the ideas you've taken from other sources to come up with something unique to your perspective. Once you've spent enough time educating yourself to the point where you feel confident in your own ability, then you can try coming up with your own interpretations without outside influence, but there's nothing wrong with seeking guidance especially when you're just starting out. There are no rules, just do what feels right for you

I don't think anyone can completely "own" an interpretation. Everyone relies on knowledge shared by everyone else. Still, I do get that enjoyment comes from that very illusion of organic, original thinking. I suggest reading things related to the subject like Jungian psychology or watching more movies similar in style to Persona.

Imo, that doesn't mean you're dumb, it just means you haven't had enough exposure to similar things that connect neatly to the movie. Intelligence is quite useless without knowledge.

I would watch it at least one more time then once I had my own firm reading of the film I would read and watch the interpretations of others.  There is so much from Persona that one can get on their own, but there is always value in reading the views of those with different life experiences.  I found explanations of the metatextual from film scholars helpful. It will still be your interpretation, but if you are anything like me then your understanding of the time period and Swedish views of psychiatry will be lacking.   If you do not want to do that then the core text of the film is certainly worth further exploration.

You came to order us around that you don't want explanations? ...okay. You should post this on one of the vapid movie subs or moviechat.com, usually here when someone brings up any title, it's a given that it'll be a broader topic for the film itself regardless of if there's a question or thesis.

You are absolutely right, interpreting and searching for deeper meaning absolutely can elevate opinion on film. I agree with all you said. But i suggest that you always do that after initial watch. At least that is what i do.
It hasn't, at least for now!
You think watching Persona entitles you to plow the riches of my Emersonian mind?
Entitles me?!

Understanding a movie is only one way to "think" about it.  The mental apparatus of a human being can do far more than analyze stuff or solve puzzles.

I understand aspects of the solar system.  I enjoy sunrises--they are beautiful.  The two are not the same.

I understand reproduction.  I enjoy sex.  The two are not the same.

I understand religious history.  Encountering a god offers awe, the sublime, Mystery.  The two are not the same.

A viewer may not need to choose among the many ways to "think" about a movie but it can simplify certain aspects of putting his experience into words that another viewer might appreciate.

By analogy, Tarkovsky complained that viewers wanted explanations of the things in his movies but that is not why he created his movies--to be solved as puzzles.

Bergman's views on Persona are of no value to you if you want to create your own.

You should not be afraid to seek out interpretations online: there are several insightful Youtube videos, hundreds of Letterboxd reviews, and other analyses on random websites that illuminate the film. After watching Persona twice and consuming some of that content, I watched a third time and ended up writing extensive notes, including notes inspired by online reviews. (I currently have 12,000 words of notes and am writing an enormous paper on Persona.) Reading others' thoughts will not stifle your own interpretation- Persona is probably the deepest and densest movie ever made.
Yeees

as others have stated - I don’t think understanding is the point here - not in film watching in general and definitely not when it comes to Persona. Rather the question that should be asked is something like ”What can I learn about myself from watching Persona?”. And, ofc, no one can answer that better than yourself.

I honestly think that both you and Persona are a better off if you watch it all by yourself, as isolated as possible. Then again, it might not turn out the be a pleasant experience 😬

Nothing wrong with liking something you don't deconstruct every artistic intention/meaning of. I love a lot of French music and I don't speak a lick of the language. For me, it communicates something deeper than the literal content of the lyrics. It's a spirit, an attitude, a moment in time being expressed. That's enough for me. 

Plus a lot of artists don't even know why they do what they do or what it "means" all the time. Sometimes they just do what comes to mind to work through some vague topic and work through that in a very free from, non-literal way. I don't know about Bergman in this case, but he was clearly okay with some level of ambiguity. Embrace the open ended, and what you personally get out of something. Not everything needs to be demystified.
